This weakness has also fed through to real estate valuations. Given that housing makes up roughly 40% of the CPI basket, Torres sees sustained suppression of this component as a powerful structural disinflationary force that underpins the bullish view on bonds and equities.
quote: The other thing for inflation that's working out really well right now, Andrew, and why I think investors should be looking to buy longer term bonds is the housing element. The immigration situation in the states has it, where rent growth is essentially at a crawl and negative in many areas of the country, including the Sun Belt. And that same weakness in the rent side has transitioned to the real estate and valuation side. And with that making up roughly 40% of the consumer price index bucket, to the extent that that remains suppressed, if you get those low, lower oil prices, we could see a lot more friendly inflation data in months ahead.
episode_title: What lower inflation means for your portfolio

headline: Torres recommends buying longer-duration US bonds, citing wide spread between core CPI and 20-30 year yields plus slowing hiring in H2
reasoning: Torres argues that with core CPI at 2.6%, the 20- and 30-year bond yields above 5% represent a historically wide spread that should narrow. If Fed Chair Kevin Warsh remains hawkish and overtightens, recession probability could rise from 15% to 25%, which would push long-end rates lower. He also expects hiring to slow in the second half due to immigration restrictions depressing labour force participation to a six-year low, further supporting the bond trade. The suppressed rent growth, driven by immigration restrictions, keeps the largest CPI component subdued, reinforcing the bull case for bonds.
quote: I think that particularly at the long end, Andrew, because if Fed Chair Kevin Warsh wants to be super hawkish and wants to go all the way down to the Fed's 2% target before maybe he takes a breath and looks at the labor market picture. What happens is if Fed Chair Warsh is as hawkish as he's been saying lately, the long end will come down because then slow down, the risks start to increase. And then there is an incremental lift in recession probability. Right now we're down to 15% in the next 12 months, but that can go up to 25%... Andrew, we have a core CPI of 2.6%. How is the 20 year bond the 30 year bond up north of 5%. That is a significant spread that history says should narrow if you have slowdown concerns.

headline: Torres expects US dollar to depreciate as Fed easing expectations build under new Chair Kevin Warsh
reasoning: Torres believes that as disinflation progresses and the case for rate cuts builds, financial conditions will ease and the dollar will depreciate. He sees Warsh potentially adopting a steady posture into year end, which combined with slowing hiring data in H2, would reinforce this weaker dollar outlook. The depreciation dynamic is an ancillary view linked to his broader bullish bond and equities thesis.
quote: I think that oil comes back down and we get the inflation figures that we need, so that the fed and the new chair, Warsh, Kevin Warsh, can take a little easy on financial condition that will lead to a depreciating dollar and maybe a steady fed into year end. That's you know, there is a higher chance that that could be the case.

headline: Torres expects oil prices to decline from current levels as Trump adopts a more conciliatory posture toward Iran ahead of US midterms
reasoning: Torres sees the recent oil move from $67 to $80 as incremental rather than a panic surge, contrasting it with prior highs around $120. He argues Trump has political incentives to avoid geopolitical aggression heading into midterm elections given a narrow GOP Senate lead and expected Democrat gains in the House. A de-escalation with Iran would remove the recent oil price uplift, supporting the disinflationary trend. Lower oil combined with suppressed rent growth could produce significantly friendlier CPI prints in coming months.
quote: I must admit here, Andrew, you know, here I think that oil prices are going to decline. I think that President Trump is going to turn around and adopt a more negotiable posture and try to bridge the gap with the Iranians, at least to appease the markets heading into the midterm elections... I think that oil has been this recent uptick. Andrew has been quite modest. You know, the low recently was $67. We're up to 80. We were at 120. So this is much more of an incremental climb rather than a panic surge. I think that oil comes back down and we get the inflation figures that we need.

headline: Interactive Brokers' Jose Torres sees US equities finishing the year up ~15% on rapidly decelerating inflation and strong earnings
reasoning: Torres notes that core CPI has fallen to 2.6% and headline CPI has decelerated from 4.2% to 3.5%, with PPI also dropping sharply. He argues this disinflation trajectory could bring the Fed near its target by early 2027, setting up potential rate cuts. After three consecutive years of ~20% returns, he sees room for equities to finish the year around 15% gains. Overall joblessness remains low and hiring is still positive, supporting investor sentiment heading into earnings season.
quote: Absolutely softer than expected inflation has really been what's been able to support this market here near record highs after three consecutive years Andrew of returns of roughly 20%. Here we are at around 10% around half times. So definitely some more some space to maybe finish the year up 15% or so. The inflation data is decelerating rapidly. That's been great news for the interest rate complex Core CPI down at 2.6%. CPI decelerating from 4.2 to 3.5. PPI down significantly as well from 6.2. Down to 5.5%. You know that can quickly become a fed that's really near its target in early of 2027, Andrew. And then we can start talking about rate cuts again.
